catalog_quote: In Nʋngʋrama, stress is expressed through length and/or loudness, rather than pitch. This is because pitch is distinctive in Nʋngʋrama, while stress is not. Typically, the first syllable of a lexeme is stressed, particularly in disyllabic words of all parts-of-speech classes. This phenomenon, known as “stem-initial prominence” (Lionnet/Hyman 2018: 652), is a characteristic feature of Niger-Congo languages in the area of the Macro-Sudan Belt (cf. Idiatov/Van de Velde 2015). However, stress can also occur on syllables other than the first in lexemes with more than two syllables, such as the second syllable in trisyllabic lexemes. The data suggests that certain consonants may influence the distribution of stress, causing it to shift from the initial syllable. For example, the consonant /p/ generally occurs lexeme-initially. new_statements.rule_in_words: Longuda/Nʋngʋrama is a two-tone language (H, L; TBU = syllable) in which stress is non-contrastive and realised as length/loudness; by default the first syllable of the lexeme (stem-initial) carries the prominence, especially in disyllables; in trisyllabic and longer words stress may instead sit on the second syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: In lexemes of three or more syllables stress can fall on the second syllable, seemingly attracted by certain second-syllable onsets (/p/, /b/, /l/, /y/): e.g. Deeləmə ʃɩ̀ˈbátà 'poverty', kwàˈlálà 'elder', yàˈpɩ́lwà 'sheep' vs ˈbàmbàlà 'bow'; Gʋyʋma gʋ̀ˈbálá 'stone', zwàˈlɩ́yá 'husband' vs ˈlàràwá 'elephant'; Gwaandama mɩ̀ˈyáhà 'goat', gùrˈbílə̀ 'he-goat', gàˈpʋ́nwà 'hyena' vs ˈyáláká 'day' (p.71; author flags this as needing further research, fn.104). Elsewhere: emphatic vowel lengthening marks stress in ideophones (p.60, after Sabe 2014:32); the final syllable of a positive imperative is 'marked by stress, length and a falling contour tone' (p.67, after Newman & Newman 1974:110f.); Newman & Newman (1977b:6) report stress on the negative clitic =gá after an imperative (p.272). Note the older SIL account differs: Newman & Newman 1974 (as quoted by Pike 1982 fn.9) tie stress to tone — 'the first high tone syllable in a word is the stressed syllable' — and (p.113, quoted by Vigeland fn.105) suggest Longuda 'may be developing into a pitch-accent language'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexeme/stem ('first syllable of a lexeme', 'stem-initial prominence'); examples are citation-form nouns including their noun-class suffixes, marked with IPA ˈ. Statement covers three varieties (Deeləmə, Gʋyʋma = Guyuk, Gwaandama); data partly from Kleinewillinghöfer's recordings and speakers in Jos. Impressionistic, no acoustic measurements.
new_statements.identity_note: Vigeland 2024 describes the Nʋngʋrama/Longuda cluster (glottocode long1389, iso lnu) polylectally from three of its five varieties: Deeləmə (Deele/Jessu), Gʋyʋma (Guyuk, incl. Wala) and Gwaandama (Gwaanda/Nyuwar); the stress statement is given for the cluster as a whole with examples from all three. The older SIL sources (Newman & Newman 1974, 1977b) describe the Guyuk dialect only. Glottolog 5.1 lists no sub-dialect codes under long1389.

sources.note: Sect. 2.2.3 Stress (p.70-71): stress is realised by length/loudness not pitch (pitch is distinctive, stress is not); typically the first syllable of a lexeme is stressed (stem-initial prominence); in words of 3+ syllables it may fall on the second syllable, apparently attracted by certain C2 onsets /p b l y/ (ʃɩ̀ˈbátà, gʋ̀ˈbálá, mɩ̀ˈyáhà). Also p.60 emphatic vowel lengthening as stress; p.67 imperative-final syllable has stress+length+falling tone; p.272 Newman&Newman 1977b:6 stress on negative =gá.
